segments.english: And God said, "Let the waters swarm with swarms of living creatures, and let birds fly above the earth across the expanse of the sky."
segments.literal: and-said God swarm-(they) the-waters swarm-of creature living and-bird fly-about above the-earth above face-of expanse-of the-heavens

phrases.literal: 'above face-of expanse-of the-heavens'; Ibn Ezra, citing the Gaon: the birds fly in the open air below the expanse

grammar: יִשְׁרְצוּ is a yiqtol with jussive force: 'let the waters swarm'. It is transitive, with שֶׁרֶץ as its object.
שֶׁרֶץ is in the construct state before נֶפֶשׁ חַיָּה: 'swarmers of living creatures'.
וְעוֹף is a collective singular, and יְעוֹפֵף is a polel (intensive, repeated motion): 'fly about'.
The etnaḥta on חַיָּה divides the verse: the waters' part, then the birds' part.
עַל־הָאָרֶץ and עַל־פְּנֵי רְקִיעַ הַשָּׁמָיִם are two parallel locations of the birds; the expanse of 1:6-8 is the setting.
segments.note: Ibn Ezra reads יִשְׁרְצוּ as transitive (as in Exodus 7:28) and says the sense is 'bring forth offspring', so the English gives the waters a cognate object. 'living creatures' renders נֶפֶשׁ חַיָּה following Rashi (a being with life in it). For על פני רקיע the Gaon, cited by Ibn Ezra, takes the birds to fly in the air below the expanse; the English 'across the expanse of the sky' keeps the Hebrew's preposition without deciding this.

commentary.summary: Rashi: נֶפֶשׁ חַיָּה means 'that there be life in it' (שֶׁיְּהֵא בָהּ חַיּוּת).
Rashi: anything alive that is not tall off the ground is called שֶׁרֶץ: flies among birds, ants and worms among the vermin, mole and mouse among beasts, and all fish.

Ibn Ezra: יִשְׁרְצוּ is transitive, like 'the Nile shall swarm with frogs' (Exodus 7:28); the sense is 'offspring with height'. The birds fly 'across the face of the expanse'; the Gaon takes פני with the following noun, so the face of the heavens is below, and יְעוֹפֵף is of the form of 'until he establish' (Isaiah 62:7).

apparatus: The Gaon (cited by Ibn Ezra): עַל־פְּנֵי is 'on the face of', so the birds fly below the expanse; the plain preposition is kept in the English.

Rashi: great fish of the sea; the aggadah makes them Leviathan and his mate
adjective in agreement, with the article
feminine participle, agreeing with נֶפֶשׁ; Ibn Ezra: 'the going'

phrases.literal: 'the-sea-monsters the-great'; Rashi: great fish of the sea
'which swarmed the-waters'; the waters are the subject, the creatures what they swarmed with

grammar: The verse opens with בָּרָא, used only of God. The great sea creatures are named first, then all living things, then birds.
הָרֹמֶשֶׂת is a feminine singular participle agreeing with נֶפֶשׁ; Ibn Ezra glosses it as 'the going'.
אֲשֶׁר שָׁרְצוּ הַמַּיִם is a relative clause with no resumptive word: 'which the waters swarmed (with)'.
לְמִינֵהֶם (plural suffix) and לְמִינֵהוּ (singular suffix) divide creatures by kind; the birds are a single collective.
The accent geresh and qadma mark the relative clause as a unit; the etnaḥta falls after הַגְּדֹלִים.
segments.note: תַּנִּינִם is rendered 'sea creatures' following Rashi (great fish of the sea); 'sea monsters' would also fit the lexicon, and Rashi's aggadic Leviathan is recorded in the commentary. The suffix on לְמִינֵהֶם is plural, matching the many swimming creatures, and on לְמִינֵהוּ singular, matching the collective bird.

commentary.summary: Rashi: הַתַּנִּינִם are the great fish of the sea; in aggadah they are Leviathan and his mate, created male and female, after which the female was killed and salted for the righteous in the future, since if they bred the world could not stand before them.
Rashi: נֶפֶשׁ הַחַיָּה means 'that has life in it'.
Ibn Ezra: הָרֹמֶשֶׂת has the sense of הוֹלֶכֶת, 'going'; some say the shin stands in place of a samekh.

apparatus: Some (cited by Ibn Ezra) take the shin of הָרֹמֶשֶׂת to be a samekh, as in the verb 'to creep'; the English 'moves' fits either.

segments.english: And God blessed them, saying, "Be fruitful and multiply and fill the waters in the seas, and let the birds multiply on the land."
segments.literal: and-blessed [object-marker]-them God to-say be-fruitful and-multiply and-fill [object-marker] the-waters in-the-seas and-the-bird multiply in-the-earth

tokens.note: object marker with a plural suffix
infinitive construct with ל, introducing speech
imperative; the root is used in the Qal

grammar: Three plural imperatives, פְּרוּ וּרְבוּ וּמִלְאוּ, address the sea creatures; the birds are addressed in the third person with the jussive יִרֶב.
פְּרוּ is from פָּרָה and רְבוּ from רָבָה; the pair is a standard blessing formula.
The first blessing in Genesis is given to living creatures; the same words are spoken to humans in 1:28.
The etnaḥta on לֵאמֹר sets off the speech; the zaqef on בַּיַּמִּים divides the sea's part from the birds' part.
segments.note: Rashi reads the blessing as a response to the creatures' vulnerability (they are hunted and eaten), which the English does not need. Ibn Ezra takes the imperatives as promises ('you will be fruitful'), not commands, since this is not in their power; the English keeps the imperative and records his reading. The lexicon lists פָּרָה only in the Hiphil; the pack's parse is Qal, and the data are kept.

commentary.summary: Rashi: because creatures of the sea are diminished, caught and eaten, they needed a blessing; the land animals needed one too, but the serpent, destined for a curse, was left out so that it would not be included.
Rashi: פְּרוּ means 'make fruit', from פְּרִי.
Rashi: if the text said only 'be fruitful' one would beget one and no more; 'multiply' means one begets many.
Ibn Ezra: the sense of פְּרוּ וּרְבוּ is 'you will be fruitful, you will multiply', as in 'and die on the mountain' (Deuteronomy 32:50), because this is not in their power.

apparatus: Ibn Ezra: the imperatives are promises, not commands.

segments.english: And there was evening and there was morning, a fifth day.
segments.literal: and-was evening and-was morning day fifth

tokens.note: ordinal; no article, as for days two to five

grammar: The formula is the same as for the earlier days; the sequence evening, then morning, makes each day begin at evening.
יוֹם חֲמִישִׁי has no article: 'a fifth day', as for the second to the fifth days.
The ordinal חֲמִישִׁי is formed from the number five.
segments.note: The phrase is rendered 'a fifth day' to keep the lack of the article.
